source.title: Slamming: Training a Speech Language Model on One GPU in a Day
source.authors: Gallil Maimon; Avishai Elmakies; Yossi Adi

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates downstream speech-model scores at different compute/model scales, bearing on whether downstream performance improves with scale, but it does not measure the original claim’s held-out text-model cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses speech-language-model scaling and compares its results with performance predicted by Cuervo and Marxer, but reports no fitted power laws, held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep, or systematic compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep. Cited prediction values are not recorded as study results. Recipe ablations such as optimiser, data mix, and architecture are not rows for the claim unless they directly measure downstream performance across scale.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (speech-token LMs initialised from text LMs), the study reports downstream scores at about 10x more compute and at a larger model size under equal compute. This bears on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It fits no scaling law and reports no held-out-loss sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that high-quality speech LMs can be trained on one GPU in a day, and that the recipe keeps improving with about 10x compute. Their results exceed the compute-optimal performance predicted by the cited SLM scaling law. They advise choosing a stronger or bigger text-LM initialisation even at the cost of fewer tokens.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains speech-token language models using text-model initialisation, synthetic speech data, DPO and compute-constrained training; it does not reproduce the original text-model loss-scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model family and initialisation, data diversity and synthetic-data use, optimiser/scheduler, DPO budget, and training compute/model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Slam at 1*A5000 (358M) scores above the performance predicted by the Cuervo & Marxer SLM scaling law for that compute (78M predicted optimal). For example, tSC is 82.04 vs a predicted 70.49 (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recipe choices such as text-LM initialisation, synthetic data and DPO can put speech-LM downstream performance well above a previously fitted SLM scaling-law prediction at fixed compute.

record.problems: The scale comparison has only a few model/compute settings and reports no fitted scaling relationship or uncertainty for Table 3; the study does not measure the original claim’s held-out cross-entropy. The paper notes that actual compute efficiency varies across model architectures and implementations.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the cited predicted-optimal and prior-model scores as they are not results generated by this study. Omitted recipe ablations and other reported metrics that do not measure downstream performance scaling; no held-out-loss or power-law rows were available.

untested.parts: No held-out loss measured across orders of magnitude of parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
No small-run fit used to extrapolate to larger runs.
No systematic fixed-compute sweep with a fitted allocation exponent. Only one equal-compute pair, measured on downstream scores.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison. Model families differ in more than shape.
Speech modality, but no loss-scaling form tested.
Only two or three scale points. No fitted relation, and no prediction from pretraining loss, so the 'predictably' part is untested.
No exponent fitting. The shift of the best model size away from the cited SLM law is only qualitative (Figure 3).

missing.what: Validation perplexity vs model size within families at fixed 24h compute. The best size is ~300M (125M for OPT) versus the ~66M optimum the cited SLM law predicts; the authors attribute this possibly to TWIST initialisation but cannot isolate the cause.
Out-of-domain GenPPL on People Speech: Slam 171.84, scaled 128.78, large 117.49.
Validation perplexity vs estimated FLOPs during training, per model family, with and without TWIST initialisation.

record.verdict_notes: The cited scaling law (Cuervo & Marxer) is not one of the original sources. The scale evidence is thin: one ~10x compute step, confounded by a doubled batch size and 2 DPO epochs, and one equal-compute size comparison with small gains on the likelihood metrics. The V6 support is directional only. Model size and family comparisons in Figure 3 are confounded by family and initialisation, and the figure gives no readable numbers.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measured as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fit or large-run loss prediction.
No systematic fixed-compute sweep or fitted parameter/token allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The models use speech tokens, but the paper does not test whether held-out loss follows the same power-law form in another modality or training regime.
No prediction from pretraining loss, and no fitted quantitative relationship predicting downstream scores from scale.
No analysis of fitted scaling exponents or how fitting choices change them.

relationships.condition: Speech-token LMs (Qwen2.5 TWIST-initialised, Slam recipe): about 10x compute at 358M, and 1.3B vs 358M at equal 2*A100x48h compute
relationships.reason: All five downstream and generation metrics improve with compute (T3-SCALED-*) and with model size at equal compute (T3-LARGE-*). Only a few points, recipe tweaks confound the compute step, and no predictive fit is reported.
relationships.display_finding: All five downstream and generation metrics improved with compute and with model size at equal compute, although recipe changes confounded the compute comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Slam versus Slam (scaled) and Slam (large) on the reported Table 3 downstream and generation metrics
reader_labels.reason: All five recorded metrics move in the better direction for the scaled and large variants relative to Slam; see T3-SCALED-sBLIMP through T3-SCALED-GPTScore and T3-LARGE-sBLIMP through T3-LARGE-GPTScore. These results show improvement with scale in this setting, not a fitted predictive law.
